name: Noise Inconsistency Map
description: Creates spatial maps of noise level inconsistencies across image regions — spliced or AI-generated regions have different noise characteristics (Mahdian & Saic, 2009).
mechanism:
This method creates a spatial map of local noise levels to identify regions with inconsistent noise characteristics, indicating splicing, inpainting, or AI generation:

1. **Block-Wise Noise Estimation**: The image is divided into non-overlapping blocks of size B×B (typically 64×64). For each block, the noise standard deviation σ is estimated using the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) of wavelet coefficients: σ = MAD(HH₁) / 0.6745, where HH₁ is the finest-scale diagonal wavelet subband (Donoho & Johnstone, 1994). This estimator is robust to image content because the HH subband primarily captures noise in smooth regions.

2. **Noise Level Map Construction**: The estimated σ values are assembled into a noise level map N(i,j), where each entry represents the noise level of the corresponding block. The map is then upsampled to full resolution using bilinear interpolation. In an authentic photograph, the noise map should be approximately uniform (constant σ) or follow a signal-dependent noise model σ(I) = √(αI + β), where I is the local intensity, α represents photon shot noise, and β represents read noise.

3. **Inconsistency Detection**: The noise map is analyzed for spatial inconsistencies. The method fits the signal-dependent noise model to the global noise-intensity relationship and computes the residual R(i,j) = N(i,j) − σ̂(I(i,j)) for each block. Blocks with |R| > 3σ_R (where σ_R is the standard deviation of residuals) are flagged as inconsistent. Spliced regions typically show either higher noise (from a noisier source image) or lower noise (from a denoised or AI-generated region) compared to the global model.

4. **Connected Component Analysis**: Flagged blocks are grouped into connected regions using 8-connectivity. Small isolated detections (< 4 blocks) are suppressed as false positives. The remaining connected regions are reported as potentially manipulated areas with their estimated noise level deviation from the global model.
parameters:
Block size: 64×64 pixels
Wavelet: Daubechies db4, single level
Noise estimator: MAD of HH₁ coefficients
Noise model: signal-dependent σ(I) = √(αI + β)
Outlier threshold: 3σ_R from model prediction
Minimum region size: 4 connected blocks
Minimum image size: 256×256 pixels
accuracy: 82–90% accuracy for splicing detection with noise inconsistency. Signal-dependent noise model achieves 87% localization accuracy for tampered regions. AI-generated content detection: 80–85% (AI images often show unnaturally uniform noise). False positive rate of 5% in images with complex lighting or ISO-variable capture.
source: Mahdian, B. & Saic, S. (2009). Using Noise Inconsistencies for Blind Image Forensics. Image and Vision Computing, 27(10), 1497–1503.
useCase: Detecting spliced regions with different noise characteristics from the surrounding image. Identifying AI-generated or denoised regions that lack natural camera noise. Estimating camera sensor characteristics (shot noise, read noise) for source identification. Localizing inpainted or cloned regions with inconsistent noise levels.
strengths:
• Noise is a fundamental physical property of cameras — highly reliable for splice detection
• MAD-based estimation is robust to image content (edges, textures)
• Signal-dependent model accounts for natural intensity-noise relationship
• Produces interpretable spatial visualization of noise anomalies
• Works on both RAW and JPEG images
limitations:
• Heavy JPEG compression introduces quantization noise that masks sensor noise differences
• Images resized significantly lose noise characteristics
• Some AI generators add synthetic noise to match natural noise profiles
• Uniform flat regions provide unreliable noise estimates (insufficient texture)
• Multiple exposures or HDR bracketing create legitimate noise variations
